newsitem.title: USA: Searchers lose hope of finding U.S. airmen alive.
newsitem.headline: Searchers lose hope of finding U.S. airmen alive.

text.p: Search crews scoured the ocean off California for bodies and wreckage from a downed U.S Air Force Reserve transport plane on Sunday but officials had given up hope of finding eight missing airmen alive.
"We're not holding out any hope of finding anyone alive," Air Force spokesman Maj. Stephen Clutter said from Portland, Oregon, where the crashed plane was based.

Two Coast Guard cutters searched the area off the northern California coast where the HC-130 Hercules, with 11 airmen on board, plunged into the Pacific Ocean on Friday evening after reporting engine and electrical problems during a training flight, Coast Guard spokesman Petty Officer Jeff Murphy said.
One Coast Guard and two Air Force helicopters that had been searching the area about 60 miles (95 kms) off Cape Mendocino, were grounded on Sunday because of poor visibility, he said.

The searchers rescued one survivor soon after the crash and recovered two bodies, but eight airmen were still missing. The crewmembers belonged to the 939th Rescue Wing's 304th Rescue Squadron, which specialises in rescues on land and sea.

Murphy said the Coast Guard had not given up the search for possible survivors but other officials said the focus of the effort was now on recovering bodies of the missing crew as well as wreckage to help determine the cause of the crash.
Chances of survival in the cold ocean waters were slim almost two days after the accident.

Clutter said the usual search time of 20 hours for survivors of ocean crashes had been doubled to 40 hours because the crew was trained in survival techniques and had survival gear on board. He said all of the bodies of the missing may never be found. The two that were recovered have not yet been formally identified, he said.

Murphy said heavy winds had spread the debris over a wide area. The Coast Guard would decide at the end of the day Sunday whether to continue the search, but the cutters would most likely continue to collect debris on Monday, he said.

The Air Force has convened a board of aviation experts to investigate the cause of the crash. It could take up to two months to complete the report, Clutter said, adding the Portland unit had halted training flights until the cause of the crash was determined.

The hulking four-engined aircraft, a military workhorse, was flying from Portland Air Base to San Diego, Calif., on a routine training mission when crewmembers reported that they had shut down one engine and that they had electrical problems, the Air Force said. Soon afterward, air traffic controllers in Oakland and Seattle lost radar and radio contact, it said.
Technical Sgt. Robert Vogel, 31, the rescued airborne communications specialist from Albany, Oregon, was flown to a northern California hospital where he was in stable condition.
